prompt.context: Our client, High Q Plastics, is an automotive parts supplier in the U.S. They primarily manufacture and sell plastic injection-molded parts -- such as grills, door handles, and decorative trim -- to automotive customers. The client has two primary revenue sources: large automotive OEMs and the aftermarket. The client has recently seen declining profits, primarily due to increased price competition from new overseas competitors in China. Annual profits have declined from $50M to $20M over the past few years.
prompt.question: What is the reason behind declining profitability? How can High Q improve profits? Can they reach $100M in profits by 2014?

clarifying_info.q: Is the overall automotive market growing or shrinking?
clarifying_info.a: Automotive sales overall are still growing steadily, driven by emerging markets.
Automotive manufacturing is leaving the U.S.

clarifying_info.q: How does High Q market position compare to competitors?
clarifying_info.a: The client is currently one of the leaders in this category.

clarifying_info.q: Where are High Q manufacturing facilities located?
What has happened to revenues over time?
clarifying_info.a: Revenues have been slowly declining over the last 5 years.

clarifying_info.q: How does High Q product quality compare to Chinese competitors?
clarifying_info.a: The client products are of higher quality than most Chinese competitors products.

clarifying_info.q: What are OEM customers doing about pricing?
clarifying_info.a: Automotive OEM customers are looking to reduce cost, driving increased price competition among parts suppliers.

exhibits.title: High Q 2010 Financials, By Facility
exhibits.shows: A table breaking down 2010 revenues, labor, material, overhead, and net profits for each of High Q four U.S. manufacturing plants (Plant A, B, C, D).

exhibits.title: 2010 U.S. Automotive Market
exhibits.shows: A pie chart showing the breakdown of 2010 U.S. automotive sales by vehicle type, with a total market size note.

exhibits.title: U.S. Automotive OEM Market -- Truck/SUV Market Share 2010 vs. 2014
exhibits.shows: A grouped bar chart comparing OEM market share in the Truck and SUV segment for 2010 and 2014 across five OEMs (Ford, GM, Chrysler, Toyota, Nissan), with additional context on High Q relationship with Toyota.

additional_info: High Q supplies 70% of Toyota business
Avg. price of High Q products sold to Toyota = $20

framework: Industry dynamics: Analyze sales volume trends; assess OEM vs. aftermarket segment size, growth, and relative profitability
Competitors: Identify who they are, their relative market share, pricing vs. client, cost structure vs. client, and any technology/quality advantage
Revenue: Examine how client prices have changed; determine if declines are across all customers and products
Costs: Identify trends in client cost structure -- increasing labor costs, material costs, or overhead

questions.prompt: Q1: What key questions would you ask an industry expert to better understand the reasons behind High Q declining profits?
questions.guidance: Candidate should structure questions MECE across four buckets: (1) Industry -- sales volume trends, OEM vs. aftermarket mix and growth, relative profitability by segment; (2) Competitors -- who they are, market share, pricing, cost structure, technology/quality advantages vs. High Q; (3) Revenue -- how prices have changed, whether declines are broad or segment-specific; (4) Costs -- trends in labor, material, and overhead costs. Strong candidates will be structured and exhaustive without overlap.

questions.prompt: Q2: The CEO wants to know if $100M in annual profits is achievable by 2014. What would you need to know, and what data would you ask for?
questions.guidance: Candidate should identify the profit formula: Profit = Q x (P - VC) - FC. They need: annual unit quantity sold (Q), selling price per unit (P), variable cost per unit (VC), and fixed costs (FC). A strong candidate frames this quantitatively and recognizes that both revenue and cost levers must be understood.

steps: Identify P = selling price per unit
Identify VC = variable cost per unit (labor + material)
Identify FC = fixed/overhead costs per plant
math.answer: Framework only at this stage; specific numbers come in Q4.

questions.prompt: Q3: What ways can you think of to increase revenues? What ways can you think of to reduce costs?
questions.guidance: Candidate should generate 2-3 concrete ideas in each category. Reduce Costs: find alternative lower-cost material sources; invest in process automation to reduce labor; consolidate multiple manufacturing sites to reduce SG&A; relocate closer to customers to reduce transportation costs. Increase Revenue: segment customers to identify those less sensitive to price; increase marketing in the aftermarket segment; negotiate long-term contracts with OEM customers to lock in volume.

questions.prompt: Q4: The client plans lean manufacturing across all 4 plants. Production will be 80% of 2010 volumes in 2014, and prices will be reduced 10% due to competition. Lean manufacturing will save an additional 20% on raw materials and 30% on labor. What is the change in profits from 2010 to 2014?
questions.guidance: Candidate must apply three compounding adjustments: volume down 20% (80% of 2010) affects revenue, labor, and material; price down 10% further reduces revenue; lean saves an additional 20% on material and 30% on labor beyond the volume reduction. Overhead is unchanged. After computing 2014 profits per plant, candidate should compare total to the $100M goal and note that even with lean manufacturing, the target is far out of reach -- a strong candidate flags the need to align client expectations.

math.setup: Revenue_2014 = Revenue_2010 x 0.80 (volume) x 0.90 (price). Labor_2014 = Labor_2010 x 0.80 (volume) x 0.70 (lean). Material_2014 = Material_2010 x 0.80 (volume) x 0.80 (lean). Overhead_2014 = Overhead_2010 (unchanged). Net Profit = Revenue - Labor - Material - Overhead.
steps: $100M target is not achievable; this result is far below the goal.
math.answer: Total 2014 profits = $28M, an improvement of $8M over 2010 $20M. The $100M target is not realistic.

questions.prompt: Q5: Based on Exhibits 2 and 3, what additional profits can High Q expect from Toyota predicted increase in market share in trucks and SUVs?
questions.guidance: Candidate must chain together multiple data points across two exhibits: calculate Toyota truck/SUV volume in 2010 and 2014, apply High Q 70% supply share, multiply by unit price to get revenues, then assess the additional revenue. Rounded answers ($13M or $14M in additional revenue) are acceptable. A strong candidate will also attempt to convert additional revenue to additional profit using the implied margin from Exhibit 1.

math.setup: Trucks and SUVs = 20% of total U.S. auto market. Toyota market share in Trucks and SUVs: 10% (2010) to 40% (2014). High Q supplies 70% of Toyota business at $20/unit avg price.
steps: Toyota Truck and SUV sales 2010 = 3.2M x 10% = 320,000
Toyota Truck and SUV sales 2014 = 3.2M x 40% = 1,280,000
High Q units sold to Toyota 2010 = 320,000 x 70% = 224,000
High Q units sold to Toyota 2014 = 1,280,000 x 70% = 896,000
math.answer: Additional revenue from Toyota growth = ~$13.4M. (2010 total profits/revenues = $20M/$400M = 5% margin; implied additional profit ~$0.67M, though the solution focuses on the revenue figure.)

questions.prompt: Q6: Please summarize your findings to the CEO, including additional opportunities to increase High Q profits over the next few years.
questions.guidance: Candidate should: (1) Restate the core problem -- declining profitability due to low-cost Chinese competition; (2) Summarize key findings -- lean manufacturing adds $8M to profits (to $28M total), still far from $100M target; Toyota share gain adds ~$13M in revenue; (3) Recommend implementing lean manufacturing; (4) Identify additional opportunities not covered in the case: consolidate the 4 plants (especially Plant D with its high overhead of $30M), pursue growth in the aftermarket segment, and diversify into plastic injection-molded parts for other industries with less price competition.

brainstorming.prompt: What ways can you think of to increase revenues AND reduce costs for High Q Plastics?

categories.name: Cost Reduction
ideas: Find alternative lower-cost material sources to reduce raw material spend
Invest in process automation to reduce labor costs
Consolidate multiple manufacturing sites (especially high-overhead Plant D) to reduce SG&A
Relocate plants closer to customers to reduce transportation costs
Implement lean manufacturing to reduce waste in labor and materials

categories.name: Revenue Growth
ideas: Segment customers by price sensitivity and protect margins with less price-sensitive customers
Increase marketing and sales focus in the aftermarket segment
Negotiate long-term volume contracts with OEM customers to stabilize revenue
Leverage quality advantage over Chinese competitors to justify premium pricing
Diversify into plastic injection-molded parts for non-automotive industries with less competition

recommendation: High Q should implement lean manufacturing across all four U.S. plants -- this adds $8M in profits (from $20M to $28M in 2014), which is a meaningful improvement but still far below the $100M target
The CEO $100M profit target for 2014 is not realistic under current assumptions and should be reset through an honest client conversation
risks: Continued price pressure from Chinese competitors could erode even the gains from lean manufacturing
Loss of U.S. automotive manufacturing volume (as production moves overseas) will compress revenue regardless of cost initiatives
Over-reliance on OEM customers (especially a single OEM like Toyota) concentrates revenue risk
next_steps: Consolidate the four plants -- especially Plant D, which has the highest overhead ($30M) and lowest profit ($2.8M in 2014)
Pursue aggressive growth in the aftermarket segment, which may have less Chinese competition and better margins
Evaluate diversification into other industries that use plastic injection-molded parts but face less price competition
Assess feasibility of moving some manufacturing offshore or near major OEM customers to reduce cost and transportation expense
